summary: Myrtletown sits just south of Eureka on the foggy, temperate coast of Humboldt County, where the average daily high hovers around 59°F year-round — a place where seasonal swings barely register and air conditioning is essentially irrelevant. That coastal mildness comes with a trade: only about 6.9 hours of sunshine per day on average, and the gray marine layer is a defining feature of daily life rather than an occasional nuisance. The area is flat to gently rolling, tucked between Humboldt Bay to the west and the redwood-draped hills to the east, giving it a compressed, end-of-the-road geography — U.S. Route 101 is the sole major artery connecting this stretch of the North Coast to the rest of California, and the nearest metro of any real size is roughly 275 miles south. With a median household income of around $55,500 against a median home value near $437,600 — roughly an 8:1 price-to-income ratio — and a poverty rate above 20%, the affordability math is tighter than it first appears for a small, remote community. Employment options orbit healthcare, timber-related industries, education, and government, largely centered in adjacent Eureka. At 2.2 square miles and just over 5,000 residents, Myrtletown is less a self-contained town than a residential appendage of Eureka — a place whose identity is inseparable from its isolation and the striking wildness that surrounds it.
